title: Survival Function, Hazard, and the At-Risk Set

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The survival function, S(t), is the probability of remaining event-free beyond time t. The hazard, h(t), is the instantaneous rate at which the event occurs at time t among those still event-free just before t. The at-risk set at time t is exactly that group: everyone who has neither had the event nor been censored before t.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Two questions can be asked of time-to-event data. The first: what fraction is still event-free by time t? That is S(t), a probability between 0 and 1 that can only fall as t increases. It describes the original group, cumulatively.

The second: of those still event-free right now, how fast are they having the event? That is h(t). Hazard is a rate, not a probability (recall the rate as events per unit of person-time, §7.4.1 and §13.4). It has a time unit and is not bounded by 1: 3 events per person-year is a sensible rate for a repeatable event, while a probability of 3 is nonsense. It is also conditional on having survived this far.

That conditioning is why hazard is not risk. Risk (1 − S(t)) is what has happened to the original group by time t. Hazard is what is happening to the survivors now. A hazard can keep rising (mortality climbing with age) when few of the original cohort remain to experience it. Using “hazard” and “risk” as synonyms is an error you will meet in survival papers.

The at-risk set is the bookkeeping behind both. A censored subject leaves it at the moment of censoring, having contributed all their event-free time. Unlike a missing value, which contributes nothing, a censored subject contributes real information up to the last contact.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: At month 12 of the conceptual 100-member study (§14.1), suppose 70 members are still enrolled and observed, 25 have dropped out and 5 have been censored earlier. The at-risk set is 70, not 100 and not 95. If 3 members drop out that month, the dropout rate for the month is 3/70 = 0.043 per member-month, measured among those who could actually drop out. The survival curve takes the same step: S(t) is multiplied by 1 − 3/70 = 67/70 = 0.957. S(12) itself is the running product of such steps for every month so far, which is exactly what the Kaplan–Meier method in §14.4 computes.

points.html: S(t): a probability, cumulative from the start, never increasing.
h(t): a rate among those still event-free at t; not a probability and not bounded by 1.
Risk and hazard are not interchangeable. Risk describes the original cohort; hazard describes the current survivors.
At-risk set at t: no event and not censored before t. Both S(t) and h(t) are computed from how this set shrinks.
